output.query: initial monotherapy choice in adult focal-onset seizures and the definition of epilepsy

results.finding: For adults with focal-onset seizures, carbamazepine, levetiracetam, phenytoin and zonisamide have Level A evidence for initial monotherapy and valproate Level B; in the elderly, gabapentin and lamotrigine have Level A evidence.
results.source: Glauser T et al., Epilepsia 2013;54:551-563 | Updated ILAE evidence review of antiepileptic drug efficacy and effectiveness as initial monotherapy for epileptic seizures and syndromes

results.finding: In newly diagnosed focal epilepsy, lamotrigine was superior to levetiracetam and zonisamide for time to treatment failure; levetiracetam was not non-inferior to lamotrigine for 12-month remission, and zonisamide was non-inferior only in the intention-to-treat analysis.
results.source: Marson A et al., Lancet 2021;397:1363-1374 | The SANAD II study of the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of levetiracetam, zonisamide, or lamotrigine for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy: an open-label, non-inferiority, multicentre, phase 4, randomised controlled trial

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, or one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over 10 years.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset (focal, generalized, unknown) and, for focal seizures, by awareness; a focal seizure may evolve to a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

output.summary: Guideline evidence for initial monotherapy in adult focal seizures is strongest for carbamazepine, levetiracetam, phenytoin and zonisamide, and SANAD II found lamotrigine the most effective of the three newer drugs tested. Epilepsy is defined by two unprovoked seizures or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures may evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the epigastric rising sensation to acid reflux or dyspepsia without neurological evaluation.
Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.
Do not prescribe zonisamide: he has a sulfonamide allergy.
required_recommendations: Start lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, chosen for their lack of interaction with metformin and amlodipine.
Test HLA-B*15:02 before any carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine.
If oxcarbazepine or carbamazepine is chosen later, check sodium at baseline and during titration.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, no meningism, back to baseline after a convulsion preceded by his habitual aura: no indication for lumbar puncture.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of left mesial temporal lobe origin with hippocampal sclerosis (focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with classic mesial-temporal aura)

differential.key_features: He blamed the spells on work stress, and some carry fear; brief stereotyped deja vu with an epigastric rising sensation, a convulsion, left temporal sharp waves and left hippocampal sclerosis exclude it.
No postural prodrome or pallor; the aura and automatisms precede the convulsion and confusion lasts 25 minutes; normal ECG.
Glucose 138 mg/dL at presentation; metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia.
Stereotyped mesial temporal aura with witnessed automatisms, a tongue bite and a concordant EEG and MRI.
Focal aura, unilateral automatisms and left anterior temporal discharges are focal.

key_clinical_evidence: Twelve to fourteen months of stereotyped deja vu with an epigastric rising sensation, misattributed to reflux, are focal aware seizures of mesial temporal origin; today's event is a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.
These recurrent unprovoked focal seizures before the convulsion meet the definition of epilepsy [ILAE_def_2014]; the single-seizure recurrence-risk rule is not needed.
Left anterior temporal sharp waves (F7 phase reversal) and TIRDA concordant with left hippocampal sclerosis localize the epilepsy to the left mesial temporal lobe.
Glucose 138 mg/dL in treated type 2 diabetes is neither hypoglycemia nor a seizure-provoking hyperglycemia.

As a South Asian patient never exposed to carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine, he needs HLA-B*15:02 testing before either; lamotrigine or levetiracetam avoid that and interact with neither metformin nor amlodipine.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Deshpande is a 52-year-old right-handed South Asian male accountant who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home this morning. His wife reports that while he was seated at the breakfast table, he suddenly stopped speaking mid-sentence, stared blankly ahead, and appeared to be making repetitive chewing motions and picking at the edge of his placemat with his right hand. This was preceded by a few seconds in which he called out that he felt "that strange déjà vu again." He was unresponsive for approximately 45 to 60 seconds, then developed bilateral arm stiffening followed by rhythmic generalized jerking of all four extremities lasting roughly 80 seconds. He was incontinent of urine during the event. Postictally, he was confused and drowsy for approximately 25 minutes before gradually reorienting.

On interview, the patient reports that for the past 12 to 14 months he has been experiencing episodic sensations that he has difficulty characterizing. He describes a sudden strong sensation of déjà vu accompanied by an uncomfortable rising sensation starting in the pit of his stomach and moving upward toward his chest, sometimes associated with a vague sense of fear. These episodes typically last 30 to 60 seconds, after which he feels momentarily foggy. He estimates they have occurred approximately once or twice per month and initially attributed them to work stress or acid reflux from his diabetes diet. He discussed the gastric sensations with his primary care physician approximately eight months ago; a proton pump inhibitor trial was initiated without change in the frequency or character of the episodes. He denies any prior convulsions, loss of consciousness, or prolonged post-ictal state prior to today. There is no history of recent head trauma, fever, CNS infection, or change in medications. He denies excessive alcohol use, missed medications, or significant sleep deprivation in the days preceding the event. He has never been evaluated by a neurologist and has never had neuroimaging or an EEG.

neurological_exam.additional: Small lateral tongue bite visible on the left side, consistent with recent seizure. No other focal neurological deficits.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin without dysmetria bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally (3 mm to 2 mm). Visual fields intact to confrontation in all four quadrants. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact to light touch and pinprick in all three divisions of CN V bilaterally. Face symmetric at rest and with activation. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait steady with normal base. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech fluent without paraphasic errors. Naming and repetition intact. Follows three-step commands without difficulty. Recall 3/3 at registration; 2/3 at five minutes, recalled the third item with phonemic cueing. Mild word-finding hesitancy noted on confrontation naming, though the patient reports this is his baseline. Cooperative and appropriate, mildly fatigued consistent with post-ictal recovery approximately 7 hours prior.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. Strength 5/5 in all muscle groups of the upper and lower extremities bilaterally. No pronator drift. No involuntary movements.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception intact in all extremities. No extinction on double simultaneous stimulation.
